questions.problem:
Consider the matrix 
$W=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 \\ -6 & 9 & -2 \\ 8 & -12 & 10\end{aligned}].$ 
Find a basis $B$ of  $\text{Col}(W).$
questions.worked_solution:
In order to find a basis of $\text{Col}(W),$ we reduce the matrix $W$ to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 \\ -6 & 9 & -2 \\ 8 & -12 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ 8 & -12 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one. 

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{3}.$ So, a basis of $\text{Col}(W)$ is $\{{w}_{1},{w}_{3}\},$ that is to say, 

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 8\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

$$

$$

The matrix $C$ is given below. Let ${c}_{1}$, ${c}_{2}$,  ${c}_{3}$, and ${c}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $C.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(C).$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${c}_{4}={x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}.$

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 & -3 & -8 \\ 3 & -4 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $C$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 & -3 & -8 \\ 3 & -4 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & -12 \\ 3 & -4 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & -12 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(C)$ is $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $4$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${c}_{4}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -8 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{4}}={{(4)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=4\cdot 3=12.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/4588c7d7ae4fd6cbc749373d83ab2d81e6a228f0cac03d5b959f4177f3f4cdf9.svg)

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express $\mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/fa2ad666a6b80eac26bad12db322fa361578d94327e230d7c520c950add78923.svg)

This gives us $x_1 \cdot x_2 = 5 \cdot 2=10.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Given Set Is a Basis of the Column Space of a Matrix With Two Rows

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining Whether a Given Set Is a Basis of the Column Space of a Matrix For a Larger Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
The matrix $A$ is given below. Let $\mathbf{a}_1$, $\mathbf{a}_2$,  $\mathbf{a}_3$, and $\mathbf{a}_4$ be the respective columns of $A.$ Determine if ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/afbd6ce90f2192c311c38ced9c1d9512c48bbf9a5e06236415ef9fe70883f9be.svg) is a basis of $\textrm{Col}(A).$ If that is the case, find $x_1 \cdot x_2$, where $\mathbf{a}_4=x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/e2ccba053acf8d050e305c3768c970ae635f4583163a867b6ef11f4e565ac1ae.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $A$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & -14 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & -14 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & 2 & -12 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2 \},$ that is to say,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/6b4306172b78c1e59bf66c8c08bf864aac2bcab65d4b1cc08ba4ddab0e5f1da3.svg)

Now, since the $4$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express $\mathbf{a}_4$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/b3681d7f6c71d06ede32616ceec12ccd71da28373ee88eab451211af5a579212.svg)

This gives us $x_1 \cdot x_2 = 2 \cdot (-3) = -6.$

Therefore, we can write

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/22d4eb11af0168d4fabc8b3ebbe1befd24620db11b6a31709472ba91bb1ed794.svg)

The vector $\mathbf{a}_3$ was not included in the basis because the $3$rd column of $A$ was not a pivot column. This means that $\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$

Now, what if we want to find the exact linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ that yields $\mathbf{a}_3?$ That is to say, we want to find $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/f3f4e0d48c58be10684eada3fd320001dc056f2d1070707d9443c9533b7b5e35.svg)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/cf66dc341420f6c399e1ad7e108986505cb349d3aba1aeaacee636e7b6ec4b94.svg)

If we reduced this matrix to the *reduced* row echelon form, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/847a4dd2e37e6e577bd9a38160f03bcb5839fbf617d76ebe0a2b42cdba0ebce1.svg)

Finally, the third column of the *reduced* matrix tells us that $x_1=3$ and $x_2=-2,$ meaning that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14144046/assets/1892b80eb017795a7420b59053b836bea894ff77b7478fc7f884de6b43384cb1.svg)

In general, if the $n$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express $\mathbf{a}_n$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. 

**Watch out!** The matrix must be written in *reduced* row echelon form (with $1$'s for pivots and $0$'s above and below the pivots), not just in a row echelon form.
